I've read the synopsis of most of his book, they all revolve around something I like to read about. I have trouble choosing which one of his books I should read first. I own a copy of Anathem and Seveneves, but some people I've talked to recommended that check out his older stuff first before I start with "complex" books like Anathem. Anyway what are your thoughts/recommendations?
What should be my first Neal Stephenson book?

If you want to start with a simpler book, Cryptonomicon is good, especially if you like history. It is fairly long though, so if you want something shorter, try Snow Crash or The Diamond Age. Those two would be good choices if you're into Science (Speculative) Fiction as well.

I think it depends on where your interests and knowledge of popular science lay. Cryptonomicon and Snow Crash are both pretty cyber. The tech is internet and network security stuff. I started with Snow Crash, but a lot of that may feel dated now. Cryptonomicon has a duel story set in two different time lines and it's fun to jump back and forth. Either should be fine for any computer/internet literate person today. Reamde is probably less science/tech based than most of the others. I feel that a lot of the research was in MMORPGs and such. It takes you from inside the next big MMO to gun fights with the Russian Mob. I just finished Seveneves myself and I think it may be my favorite. I found the science really easy to follow. Yeah there were genetics and physics and angles of trajectory and all that, but it never felt hard to follow or forced. It was helped by the fact that one of the narrators is basically Neil deGrasse Tyson and explains parts of it to you like you're just a normal person.

All that said, if you're a reader, I don't think you can go wrong. To me, the most complex parts of his books are not the science, but the writing. He does a good job of explaining the science, but if you're not used to reading giant 1000 page books, keeping up with that much story may be something you want to save until you're more comfortable with him. However, if you feel comfortable with that, just pick up the one that seems like the most fun and go for it; I don't think you can choose wrong.

Thanks, I think I'll go with Snow Crash or Cryptonomicon, whichever I can get my hands on first. These seem like the popular choice in this thread. Hopefully I should be okay with the sciency/techy parts as a math major and casual programmer. Seems like there is little more emphasis on these in his books than other authors maybe? Nevertheless can't wait to dive in!
More emphasis on it than other authors to be sure, but as a Japanese History major I never had much trouble following. You should be fine. Enjoy!
Snow crash. Just such a fun read.
Any of them, they're all great! I started with The Baroque Cycle and he became one of my favourite authors after the first couple of chapters.

Started with the Baroque cycle too, after seeing someone checking the whole series out at the library. I was intrigued by the volume... Took me a year to plough through them, was probably hooked after 30 minutes. After that I read Cryptonomicon. Listened to audiobook of Snow Crash while commuting. Addictive.

It really comes down to personal preferences, and interests.

Satire/Linguistics/90s Cyberpunk - Snow Crash

Neo Victorian revival/nano-punk - The Diamond Age Or A Young Woman's Illustrated Primer (though this is usually best after Snow Crash)

Cryptography/WWII history/cryptocurrency - Cryptonomicon

Higher level maths/logic, in addition to blend of hard science fiction with some abstract physic concepts - Anathem.

The Baroque cycle I have been told is good for fans of history. Reamde for gun nuts. Seveneves seems to be back to form into science fiction, after writing techno thrillers, and historical adventure. All of which are on my personal "to read list".

Read the backs, or the first paragraph on wikipeda on the novel, see if it is something you could get into. You own both Anathem, and Seveneves, you can just give one a go one afternoon, see if it interests you. I will say that in comparison to Anathem, his other works tend to be "more exciting" from the get-go. I highly recommend giving Anathem a proper go at some point, even if you don't initially "get into it", and read one of his "friendlier" books first to get a sense of his style.

These aren't complex like Gravity's Rainbow or Finnegan's Wake, they're complex in content and assume some level of scientific literacy or aspiration to it. These aren't books that require learning how to read them before one can enjoy them.

If you liked The Martian, try Seveneves: it's got deeper science and a lot more information, but the scale for everything is much larger. There's really no prerequisitive for Stephenson, other than curiosity. If you have that you'll be good with whatever you choose.
